blocks.text: In A1 you have learned the numbers In front of a name, however, the Arabic number follows its own rules, among the most famous of grammar: from three to ten takes the form \"opposed" to the genus of name ( ⁧ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ⁩ but ⁧ثَلَاثُ سَيَّارَاتٍ⁩ ), and the counted name changes number and case depending on the digit (plural genitive after 3–10, singular accusative after 11–99, singular genitive after 100 and 1000). In this unit learn the complete system up to millions, years, percentages, fractions, prices in Arab currencies and order them over ten. The rules are many: the objective of A2 is use them well with the most frequent names (days, years, hours, people, euros) and recognize the rest. Two weeks.

blocks.text: “One” uses the singular noun; “two” uses the dual. Not said. ⁧وَاحِد كِتَاب⁩ . ⁧وَاحِد⁩ and ⁧اِثْنَان⁩ are added after the name, as adjectives that agree, only to insist on the number: ⁧غُرْفَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ فَقَطْ⁩ One room is one. One of them, one of them. ⁧أَحَدُ⁩ ( m.) / ⁧إِحْدَى⁩ (f.) + plural determined, in iḍāfa: ⁧أَحَدُ الطُّلَّابِ⁩ • one of the students • ⁧إِحْدَى المُوَظَّفَاتِ⁩ (a) one of the employees (a) ⁧أَحَدُهُمْ⁩ One of them is. In the news it is very frequent: ⁧أَحَدُ المَسْؤُولِينَ⁩ • a person in charge.
Three rules:
1. The number comes first and the name follows it in iḍāfa, to the undetermined plural genitive: ⁧ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ⁩ .

2. Polarity. If the singular name is masculine, the number has the ⁧ة⁩ ; If it's feminine, it doesn't. Count on singular, not plural: ⁧رَجُل⁩ ( m.) → ⁧خَمْسَةُ رِجَالٍ⁩ ; ⁧اِمْرَأَة⁩ ( f.) → ⁧خَمْسُ نِسَاءٍ⁩ ; ⁧لَيْلَة⁩ ( f.) → ⁧سَبْعُ لَيَالٍ⁩ , although ⁧لَيَالٍ⁩ has no ⁧ة⁩ .

3. The number declines as a name: ⁧رَأَيْتُ ثَلَاثَةَ رِجَالٍ⁩ I saw three men. ⁧فِي خَمْسَةِ أَيَّامٍ⁩ In five days. The name stays with the genitive. Attention to shapes. ⁧عَشَرَةُ⁩ ( ʿašaratu) with male children, ⁧عَشْرُ⁩ ( ʿašru) with the female: also the vowel changes. ⁧ثَمَانِيَةُ⁩ with males, ⁧ثَمَانِي⁩ ( ṯamānī) with women. The diptotes remain such: ⁧سَبْعَةُ أَسَابِيعَ⁩ , ⁧تِسْعُ دَقَائِقَ⁩ ( A2-08). With the article the number usually follows the name as adjective: ⁧الأَيَّامُ الثَّلَاثَةُ⁩ The three-day period shall be: ⁧السَّنَوَاتُ الخَمْسُ⁩ The five years are the same. It is also found ⁧ثَلَاثَةُ الأَيَّامِ⁩ , less frequent. A trick to remember. With the male names the number appears feminine, and vice versa. Think about ⁧ثَلَاثَةُ أَيَّامٍ⁩ and ⁧ثَلَاثُ سَاعَاتٍ⁩ like models and repeat them until they sound natural.
19 ⁧تِسْعَ عَشْرَةَ صَفْحَةًتِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا⁩
The rules:
1. The name goes to the singular indeterminate accusative: ⁧خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ يَوْمًا⁩ (Lett. 15 as per day).
2. 11 and 12 they agree in both parts: ⁧أَحَدَ عَشَرَ⁩ ( m.) / ⁧إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ⁩ ( f.).
3. From 13 a 19 the unit follows polarity (as 3–9), the second part shall agree: ⁧ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ يَوْمًا⁩ , ⁧ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً⁩ .

4. The two sides end up in -a and don't decline, except 12: ⁧اِثْنَا عَشَرَ⁩ (name) / ⁧اِثْنَيْ عَشَرَ⁩ (genitive and The Court ruled: ⁧عَشَرَ⁩ and ⁧عَشْرَةَ⁩ . In numbers 11–19, with the male they say ʿašara (without ⁧ة⁩ ), with women ʿašrata (with ⁧ة⁩ and without vowel on the š): the opposite of what happens with the 10 alone.
The tens have only one form for the two genera and decline as a healthy plural: -ūna the name, -īna to the genitive and the accusative.
The composite numbers are called units + ⁧وَ⁩ + 10 , as in German (- 1 and 20 ,):
99 ⁧تِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ دَقِيقَةًتِسْعَةٌ وَتِسْعُونَ يُورُو⁩

The name goes to the singular accusative, as after 11–19. The unit follows the rules of 1–2 (agreement) and 3–9 (polarity); both sides decline: ⁧فِي خَمْسَةٍ وَعِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا⁩ In twenty-five days. How many? ⁧كَمْ⁩ followed by the name to the singular accusative, as after 11–99: ⁧كَمْ طَالِبًا فِي الصَّفِّ؟⁩ How many students are there in the classroom? ⁧كَمْ سَنَةً عِشْتَ فِي القَاهِرَةِ؟⁩ How many years have you lived in Cairo?
